entry.title: Who learns to code when AI writes the code?
entry.summary: AI writes the easy code that junior developers used to learn on. What teams lose when nobody struggles with the basics, and what tech leads can do.
entry.content:
Most of us learned to code on boring tickets. A form that did not validate. A query that was slow. A bug that only happened on Fridays. Today an AI tool closes most of those tickets in a minute.

That is good for the backlog. I am not sure it is good for the people who should learn from those tickets.

I lead release engineering and developer experience, and I mentor engineers. I also use AI tools every day. I call AI a very fast junior colleague. So here is the question that bothers me. If the fast junior colleague takes all the junior work, where do the next seniors come from?

#The easy tickets were the school

Nobody planned it this way, but the small tasks were the training. A junior developer got a simple bug. They read code they did not write. They added a log line, ran it, and were wrong twice. On the third try they understood the system a little better.

That slow loop built three things that I look for in a senior engineer. They can read unfamiliar code. They can debug without a guess. They know when a result looks wrong before a test tells them.

AI tools skip the loop. You describe the problem and get a fix that often works. You learn that the fix works. You do not learn why the bug was there.

#"Juniors will learn faster with AI"

This is the most common answer I hear, and I partly agree. A patient tool that explains any line of code is a great teacher. I wish I had one ten years ago.

But "can learn" and "does learn" are different things. In early 2026, Anthropic published a small randomised study with 52 mostly junior engineers. They learned a Python library that was new to them. One group had an AI assistant, and one group wrote the code by hand.

The AI group finished about two minutes faster, and that difference was not significant. On the quiz after the task, the AI group scored 50% and the hand-coding group scored 67%. The biggest gap was on debugging questions.

The detail I find most useful is in the same study. Some people in the AI group still scored well. They asked for explanations, or they asked only conceptual questions and fixed their own errors. The people who handed the whole task to the AI scored the lowest.

So the tool is not the problem. The way people use it is the problem. A junior under deadline pressure will usually take the fastest path. Most people would.

#"We will not need many juniors anyway"

The second answer is colder. AI writes the simple code, so teams hire fewer juniors. Some data points that way. A Stanford paper by Brynjolfsson, Chandar and Chen found that employment fell for young workers in jobs where AI can automate tasks. Software developers are in that group. The authors say the results are early and do not prove a cause.

I think this answer is wrong even if the hiring numbers are right. Every senior engineer was a junior first. A team that stops training juniors spends its seniors and does not replace them. The bill arrives years later, when nobody remembers why.

There is a second problem. The work does not get simpler for the seniors, because somebody must still review the AI output.

A study from METR gave experienced open-source developers real tasks in their own large projects. Before the study they expected AI to make them 24% faster. With AI, they were 19% slower. Reviewing and fixing the AI suggestions took much of the time.

Review is a senior skill. It needs exactly the judgement that the boring tickets used to build.

#What the struggle teaches

I want to be precise here. I do not think pain is good on its own. Nobody needs to write a CSV parser by hand to become a good engineer.

The useful struggle is smaller and more specific. It is the moment when you have a theory, you test it, and the result says you are wrong. That moment builds a mental model of the system. An AI fix that works on the first try removes that moment.

In release engineering I see the same pattern from the other side. Incidents happen in the space between what the code does and what people think it does. An engineer who never debugged by hand has a bigger space like that. I can't prove that with data. It is what I expect, and it worries me.

#What tech leads can do

Don't ban AI tools for juniors. That is silly, and they will use them anyway. Change what you ask for instead.

Ask juniors to explain each change in the pull request, in their own words. What was wrong, and why does this fix it? If the explanation is vague, talk before the merge. The code may be fine. The understanding is what you review.

Keep some tasks for learning. A small, real bug with no deadline is the best kind. The rule is simple. Find the cause first, then use any tool for the fix.

Ask for the tests before the code. I think tests are the honest way to agree on what "correct" means. A junior who writes the test first must understand the problem before the AI touches it. I use the same habit in my own side projects with AI.

Pair with them on debugging. Not on features, on bugs. Watching how someone else forms a theory teaches more than a long document.

None of this is new. It is normal mentoring. The difference is that the work no longer teaches by default. Now somebody has to plan it.

If you are a junior developer, use AI to ask "why?" more often than "fix this". If you lead a team, who in your team is learning right now, and on which tasks? Tell me how you do it.

entry.title: HIT-6, MIDAS and MSQ-21 in plain words
entry.summary: Your neurologist may hand you three short questionnaires. Here is what HIT-6, MIDAS and MSQ measure, how they are scored, and why a diary helps.
entry.content:
A migraine appointment is short. The doctor has a few minutes, and you have years of bad days to describe. So many clinics use a questionnaire. It turns the bad days into a number that a doctor can compare over time.

Three questionnaires come up again and again: HIT-6, MIDAS and MSQ. I know them because Migraine.Club builds its doctor summaries on them. This post explains each one in plain words. I am an engineer, not a doctor, so I will stay with how the tools work.

This is not medical advice. Talk to your doctor.

#HIT-6: how much migraine gets in the way

HIT-6 stands for Headache Impact Test, with six questions. Each question asks how often headache affects something in your life. Examples are pain, daily activities, and feeling tired or irritated. You answer from "never" to "always".

Each answer gives points, and the points add up to a total between 36 and 78. A higher number means a bigger impact. Clinical trial documents, such as this statistical analysis plan, describe the scoring and the usual four groups. The groups go from "little or no impact" (49 or less) to "severe impact" (60 or more).

HIT-6 looks at a recent period, about the last four weeks. It does not count your attacks. Two people with the same number can live very different lives. That is fine, because the test measures impact, not frequency.

#MIDAS: how many days you lose

MIDAS stands for Migraine Disability Assessment. It has five questions about the last three months. The first questions ask how many days you could not work or study, or how many days you did much less because of headache. Other questions cover housework and free time.

You add up the days. The total puts you in one of four grades, from little or no disability to severe disability. The lowest grade is 0 to 5 days. The highest is 21 days or more.

I like MIDAS because the unit is easy to understand. A day is a day. But look at the long window. Three months is a long time to remember. If you answer from memory, I think the number can easily be too low or too high.

#MSQ: how migraine feels in daily life

MSQ means Migraine-Specific Quality of Life Questionnaire. The version I know has 14 questions, and doctors often call it version 2.1. It looks at the last four weeks.

The questions fall into three groups. One group asks how migraine limits your daily tasks. One group asks how migraine stops you from doing things, for example when you cancel a plan or stay away from people. The last group asks about feelings, such as frustration. A validation study of the Greek version describes this structure.

Each group gets a score from 0 to 100. Here the direction flips. A higher MSQ score means a better quality of life. I find this easy to get wrong, so read the arrow on every chart.

#One question each, side by side

The three tests are not rivals. They ask three different questions.

HIT-6 asks "how bad is the impact?" MIDAS asks "how many days did I lose?" MSQ asks "how does migraine change my life?"

A doctor may use one, two or all three. Some clinical trials use them as well, to see if a treatment changes the numbers. I will not say which test is "best". It depends on the question the doctor wants to answer.

#Why memory makes these tests weak

All three tests ask you to remember. That is the weak point, and I think it is the part most people miss.

I think memory favours the worst attack and the most recent week. The mild days fade. A form in a waiting room, filled in within five minutes, may tell you more about that day than about the last three months. This is my opinion, not a result from a study.

A diary fixes this in a simple way. You write each attack down on the day. You note the date, the length, and whether you could work. At the end of the month the facts are already there. The questionnaire becomes a check of the diary, not a guess.

That is the idea behind the summaries in Migraine.Club. The app does the counting, so you can focus on the answers. Be careful with any app that shows a score, including mine. A score is only as good as its inputs, so I label how sure the app is.

#What to bring to the appointment

If you have an appointment soon, keep the list short.

  • Bring your diary, or a list of attack dates for the last three months.
  • Count the days you lost to migraine, and note the number.
  • Write down how many days you took medicine, because the doctor will ask. Do not change any dose on your own.
  • Write your two biggest worries.

Do not try to match a "good" score. The numbers are for your doctor, not for a prize. If you want to learn more about migraine in general, the International Headache Society is a good place to start.

Have you filled in one of these forms? Did the number match your life? Tell me.

entry.title: Boring deploys are the goal
entry.summary: A good release is a non-event. Here is how small batches, automation and fast rollback make deploys boring, and what that looks like on a dashboard.
entry.content:
If your release is exciting, something is wrong. Nobody should clap when a deploy ends. Nobody should hold their breath while it runs.

I work in release engineering. My job is to make releases dull. I think this is the best compliment a deploy can get: "Did that already go out?"

#Why big releases hurt

A big release collects many changes. Each change is small and safe on its own. Together they are a pile that nobody can hold in their head.

When the pile breaks something, the question is "which change did it?" That question is slow to answer. You have a long diff, many authors, and a clock that runs while users wait.

Martin Fowler has a short note on this: when something is painful, do it more often. Pain pushes the team to make the step easier. Rare releases make the pain bigger and the habit weaker.

I have seen teams react to a bad release with more sign-offs and more meetings. I understand why. But I don't think it works. A manual sign-off asks a person to judge a huge change in an hour. That person cannot do it well. The ritual only moves the blame.

#Small batches do most of the work

The best tool I know is also the simplest. Ship less per deploy.

A deploy with one small change has a short list of suspects. If it fails, the cause is almost always that change. You find it in minutes, not hours. You also revert a small change with little fear.

This is why I say small changes are safe changes. It is not a slogan for me. It is how I decide where to spend time. I would rather make deploys cheap than make reviews longer.

Small batches ask for a few habits in the team:

  • Merge to the main branch often, in small pieces.
  • Keep unfinished work behind a switch, so it can ship but stay off.
  • Never let a change wait for a "release day".

#Automate the steps you fear

Pick the step in your release that makes people nervous. Often it is the step a person does by hand, from memory, once a week. Automate that step first.

A script does not forget the third item on the checklist. It does the same thing at 10:00 on Tuesday and at 17:45 on Friday. That is what I want from a release. The same result, every time.

Automation also makes the process visible. You can read it, review it and improve it. A hand-made process lives in one person's head, and that person goes on holiday.

I am not saying "remove all humans". People still decide what to ship and when to stop. But a person should not be the part that carries the steps. A person should be the part that checks the result.

#Make rollback the easy path

Every deploy needs a way back that is faster than the way forward.

The Google SRE book describes release engineering as a discipline of its own. One idea there matches my own view: releases should be repeatable and automated, so that nobody depends on one person's tricks.

Rollback puts this idea to the test. If going back means a long meeting, people will wait and hope. If going back means one command, people will use it early. Early rollback is cheap. Late rollback is a bad day.

Before any release I ask one question. "How do we undo this, and how long does it take?" If the answer is vague, the release is not ready. Database changes are the hard case here, because a schema change does not always revert as easily as code. I plan those in steps, and I will write about that in a later post.

#What boring looks like on a dashboard

A boring deploy has a clear signature in the data. The DORA research names four measures. How often you deploy. How long a change takes to reach production. How often a deploy fails. How fast you recover.

I look at them as a group. If I only watch speed, I may push teams to rush. If I only watch failures, I may push them to stop deploying. The healthy picture has many small deploys, a short wait from commit to production, few failures, and short recovery.

On a good day, the dashboard is flat and quiet. The deploy count goes up in small steps. The error line stays where it was. Nobody opens a channel for an incident.

That flat line is the goal. It looks like nothing happened. A lot of work went into making nothing happen.

#The hard part is not technical

I will be honest. The tools are not the main problem. Most teams I know can set up a pipeline.

The hard part is trust. A manager who has seen a bad release will ask for a gate. A developer who got blamed once will batch changes "to be safe". Both choices are human, and both make releases riskier.

So I spend as much time on blameless incident reviews as on pipelines. If a failure leads to blame, people hide risk. If it leads to a fix in the process, people ship smaller things, more often.

What is the most boring deploy you remember? Tell me. I like those stories.

entry.title: How I build side projects with AI: 7 rules that work
entry.summary: How I build real side projects with AI coding tools, and what I recommend. Keep the scope small, write the spec first, test everything, and stay the engineer.
entry.content:
I build side projects with AI tools. Three of them are live now. Migraine.Club is a migraine diary that makes summaries for doctors. Parley is a terminal app where AI investor personas debate a stock. Claude Life OS is a Claude skill for personal paperwork.

AI did not build these projects for me. It changed how I build them. Some things got much faster. Some things I now do more carefully than before.

Here are the seven rules that I follow. Each rule has what I do, and what I recommend to you.

#1. Start with a problem, not with a tool

I never start with "I want to build something with AI". I start with a problem that I, or people near me, have.

Migraine.Club started with one question. How can a person show their doctor clear data about their migraines? Every feature answers that question: the one-tap log, the doctor summary, and the dim mode for bad days.

My recommendation: write your problem in one sentence before you open any tool. When the problem is clear, the AI gets clear instructions. When the problem is not clear, the AI writes a lot of code that nobody needs.

#2. Write the spec before the prompt

AI is fast. A bad plan also becomes code fast.

Now I write a short spec before I ask for code. It is one page or less. It has four parts:

  • who the user is, and what their problem is,
  • what the feature must do,
  • what the feature must not do,
  • how I will know that it works.

Then I give the spec to the AI. The result is much better. And I have something to check the result against.

My recommendation: keep the specs in the repository, next to the code. The next prompt can use them too.

#3. Keep each task small

I give the AI one small task at a time. "Add a button that exports the last 30 days as a PDF" is a good task. "Build the reports module" is not a good task.

Small tasks give small diffs. I can read a small diff in two minutes. Nobody really reads a diff with 2,000 lines. That is how bugs get into production.

My recommendation: if you cannot describe the task in two sentences, split it. Release engineering taught me the same rule. Small changes are safe changes.

#4. You are still the engineer

The AI writes the code. I own the code.

I read every diff. I run it. I ask "why?" when something looks strange. If I cannot explain a piece of code, I do not merge it.

AI sounds very sure, also when it is wrong. It can use an API that does not exist. It can remove a check "to make the code simpler".

My recommendation: review AI code like code from a new colleague. Be friendly, but check everything. You are the last check before your users.

#5. Let the tests decide

For me, tests are the best way to agree with an AI about what "correct" means.

I ask for the tests first, or together with the code. Then I run them. When a test fails, I give the error output back to the AI. This loop is fast and honest. A test does not care how sure the answer sounds.

This is very important in Migraine.Club. The app shows scores like HIT-6 and MIDAS. A wrong score is worse than no score.

My recommendation: everything that calculates or stores data needs tests with known inputs and known results, before real people see it.

#6. Make the hard decisions yourself

Some decisions are not for the AI: privacy, security, the data model, and what the product promises to its users.

Migraine.Club is privacy-first. I made that decision on day one, and it shaped everything after it. Parley is local-first for a similar reason. A tool does not know what your users trust you with.

My recommendation: write these decisions in your spec as rules. Then the AI follows them, and you can see quickly when it does not.

#7. Ship early, then make it better

A side project that is not online helps nobody. I put a first version live as soon as it does one thing well.

Real users show you what is important. Usually it is not what you expected. Parley is a terminal app. It does not need a website to be useful.

My recommendation: pick the smallest form that works. A small web app or a command-line tool is enough for version one.

#What AI changed for me

Before AI tools, my side projects often stopped in the boring middle part. Forms, settings pages, configuration, glue code. Now that part takes evenings, not weeks.

So my time goes to the parts that matter: the problem, the decisions and the review.

I think of AI as a very fast junior colleague. I give it clear tasks. I check its work. I keep the responsibility.

#My checklist

  • One problem, in one sentence.
  • A one-page spec before the first prompt.
  • One small task per prompt.
  • Read and run every diff.
  • Tests for everything that calculates or stores data.
  • Privacy and security decisions made by you.
  • A live first version, as early as possible.

Do you build something with AI in your free time? Tell me about it. I read every message.
